matter (rūpa) is not identical to earth.
If one were to challenge this point, it would entail the fault of contradicting one's own tenet.
Commentary:
Regarding the statement, "Nor is it the case that earth and so forth are what is intended here," the treatise says, "Nor is it that the eye sees real earth and so forth.
This means that earth and so forth are not subsumed under the category of real entities as perceived by the eye.
This is the meaning of "this intention," which refers to the principle of mutual analogy between this and that.
[Commentary].
Regarding the statement that "karma reaches the nature of the three [realms] and form (*rūpa*)":
the Great Existence (*mahābhūta*) and the derivative elements (*upādāya-rūpa*) constitute the nature of form.
Commentary.

Regarding the statement that "when the time for apprehending sound arrives, it is designated as the ear-faculty," this is because the function of apprehending sound arises from the space adjacent to the body. Question: Is the ear-faculty permanent? Answer: The ear is itself empty space.
Therefore, the ear is either permanent or impermanent;
just as the subtle element (*tanmātra*) produced from the eternal subtle element is impermanent.
However, the former interpretation is superior, for that treatise states that the ear is itself empty.
Therefore,
it differs in meaning from "subtle" (*miao*).
[Commentary].
Regarding the phrase "using space as an analogy up to the number [of atoms]":
the character "number" (數) is likely an error;
it should be the character "not" (不).
Although space, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and so forth are not separate from the mind, they cannot be used as analogies.
Why is this? Space, analytical cessation, and so forth are phenomena that belong to the Buddha’s Dharma.
Now, we employ the logic of another school (*parapakṣa*) as an inference (*anumāna*).
One must not take one's own [school’s] dharmas, such as analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), as the example.
Therefore, the commentary states: "employing the inference of another school."
This explains the reason.
If it were not so, where previously was there an analogy for analytical cessation (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) such that one could speak of "number"?
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "although there may be faults such as being 'other' or 'one of many,'" in the Buddha-dharma,
"other" refers to that which is external to the Dharma.
Because they are outsiders (*tīrthika*).
The rest may be understood by analogy.
Commentary.
Regarding the statement that "the remaining eight phrases, each individually excluded, constitute eight formal inferences," there is an interpretation that within these nine phrases,
whichever phrase one excludes serves as the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the reason (*hetu*).
The statement "not real," and so forth,
does not indicate a large quantity. Why is this so?
Furthermore, regarding the initial thesis’s statement that "virtues and so forth are equal," are they all equal when excluding the phrase "inexpressible"?
If they are not equal, then they are not exhaustive.
If it is said that "the reason (*hetu*) is not fixed" and so forth,
then all the others are what is being compared.
That is to say, by means of a single thesis and reason, one is already able to establish that the eight propositions being compared do not exist apart from consciousness.
Furthermore, the remaining [points] constitute the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the failure due to mutual support of the characteristics of the offense (*āpatti-lakṣaṇa*).
Since the former has already been established, these initial measures collectively form eight propositions (*pada*).
Subsequently, one is established separately, making two measures in total. Detailed explanation:
The intent of the commentary states that within these nine propositions, the removal of any single one constitutes a valid measure (*pramāṇa*);
it is not restricted solely to the two cases of "not being real" (*asat*) and "being dual" (*dvaya*).
The other phrases all possess the sense of being "removable" as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Fearing that those who are confused might rely on the literal text and become dogmatically attached—thinking that what is neither real nor dual can alone constitute valid cognition while everything else cannot—it is said that there are eight types of valid cognition.
Alternatively, there may be distinct meanings such as "two combined" and so forth based on the number of syllables;
however, this does not necessitate that they be treated as such. Furthermore, it is not stated that there is no fault in the quantity being "two combined" and so forth.
This statement was made in order to cause students to develop a distinct understanding.
Regarding the argument concerning "existence" and so forth as they are grasped by those [opponents]:

Question: If one uses the objection that [an argument] cannot be without a cause to challenge another, then even those phenomena within the Buddha’s Dharma that possess substantial existence would fail to be established. Another’s measure (pramāṇa) challenges this, saying:
"Your sound..."
It must be that there is no separate intrinsic nature (svabhāva) external to form (rūpa), because you admit it is not non-existent, just like form and so forth. [Response:
Within your own thesis, this contradicts your own scriptures, common worldly consensus, direct perception (pratyakṣa), and your own words.
"Do you not admit that sound exists apart from form?
Below, this same objection applies to the real cause of difference;
the refutation is likewise the same. Thus the opponent further objects.
Your seventh and eighth consciousnesses must lack a distinct intrinsic nature apart from the six consciousnesses;
for you admit that they are of the nature of consciousness and are not non-existent.
Just like the visual consciousness and the others,
if it were separated from the six consciousnesses,
it would not possess the nature of consciousness.
Because it allows for the difference from the six consciousnesses,
like [the case of] absolute non-existence and so forth;
thus, the three members of the syllogism are complete.
7. There should be no seven or eight [consciousnesses]. Answer: The preceding reason has the fault of being definitively contradictory.
The proof of contradiction is as follows:
Regarding the seven or eight consciousnesses themselves...
It must possess a distinct self-substance apart from the six consciousnesses,
because it is admitted to be the co-existent faculty (*sahabhū-indriya*) for other consciousnesses,
just like the eye-faculty and the others.
Furthermore, the subsequent inference has the fallacy of being partially contradicted by another [scriptural] position (*pakṣaikadeśa-bādhita*).
In the Buddha’s Dharma, it is not admitted that the eighth consciousness and the six [consciousnesses] are invariably dissociated.
Consequently, the reason (*hetu*) also suffers from the fallacy of being partially contradicted by another [position].
The eight [reasons] constitute six bases because they are not necessarily distinct.
Furthermore, while the conventional has distinctions, the ultimate is without distinction.
Since these are established as mere semblances, how could they possess the three members [of a syllogism]?
Therefore, the doctrine of seven or eight consciousnesses is established.
This should be further examined with careful reflection.
[Commentary]
To refute the contradiction with what is certain,
the opponent formulates the following proof:
"That which is spoken of as having existence..."
"Distinctness" (*anyathātva*) and so forth possess a separate intrinsic nature from "reality" (*tattva*) and the other three,
because— excluding the statement of non-existence— they are subsumed under one of the remaining six propositions,
just like the proposition of "difference" (*anyatva*). Some say:
There is the nature of existence (sattā). It must necessarily exist as something distinct from the three categories,
such as substance (dravya) and so forth, because it is not subsumed under substance and the others.
Regarding the phrase "distinct from others," it means that there exists a separate substantial entity. If this were the case,
the reason would incur the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Is it like the case where "real" (*satya*) and so forth do not include [the category of] existence, yet there is a separate substantial entity for that existence?
Or is it like the case where "non-existent" (*asat*) and so forth do not include [the category of] existence, yet there is no separate substantial entity for that non-existence?
Therefore, one should rely on the former position.
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "this difficulty is always equal," this refers to the words of the Master of the Treatise.
Although you previously understood my position, I now rebuke you:
existence and non-existence are always equal.
By what means can you now dispel my objection that existence and non-existence are indeed equal?
How can the author of the treatise dispel the external objection?

The previous interpretation is the primary one. According to another view, if the Vaiśeṣika were to defend their position by arguing that because a dharma possesses "existence" (sattā), the objection that it would otherwise be non-existent is thereby removed, then [the opponent] should likewise respond:
"Your [categories of] form and so forth must also exist, because they depend on causes. Thus, they cannot be non-existent.
Turtle hair does not exist because it lacks a dependent cause;
since you admit that existent phenomena arise from causes,
non-existence cannot fail to depend on [the absence of] such causes.
I also have a teaching: that because something exists, it exists;
there is no non-existence that does not depend upon non-existence for its being non-existent. The explanation says: In my teaching, dharmas possess cause and effect.
Both cause and effect arise and perish together.
"Since you arise from conditioned causes, you ought not to be a single, permanent entity. [The opponent] replies: "Your interpretation of the meaning is excellent, but your phrasing is deficient."
It may be said that even a white jade disc still possesses a flaw.
Why is this so? Because the principle of non-action (wuwei) serves as both the fruit of dissociation (visamyoga-phala) and the efficient cause (kāraṇa-hetu).
How could it be that [the self] is subject to arising and ceasing?
If one relies on the scriptural passage concerning conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), there is no such distinction;
for although other [factors], such as substance (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and activities (*karman*), arise from causes, [the self is not like them].
He also admits for himself that there is impermanence;
how could these not support one another? If you single out impermanence to challenge him, [you contradict your own position].
Why, then, is there no such distinction?
Therefore, one should now say:
"In my view, conditioned phenomena possess causes and effects."
If cause and effect arise and perish simultaneously,
then since the real entities (*satya*) and so forth would arise from causes,
those real entities and so forth should likewise not be unitary or eternal.
Commentary:

"There is nothing here that is also of the nature of identity or difference" means that this nature of identity and difference is not merely the nature of those [categories] such as substance (*dravya*) and so forth.
Furthermore, its own essence is neither identical nor different.
Therefore, it is said "also. To explain in detail:
perhaps it existed previously as well.
Since the previously refuted nature of being unreal and so forth applies equally to both identity and difference,
the treatise uses the word "also."
Commentary:
Regarding the statement that "in this [position] there are no faults such as contradiction with one's own words," one interpretation holds that these words refer to what you yourself maintain.
Although this may demonstrate what is not accepted by [the proponent] himself,
the two terms "dharma" and "dharmin" are contradictory; thus,
one cannot claim that there is no fault of contradicting one's own words.

Therefore, the thesis (*pakṣa*) should be stated as: "Your [proposition that] sameness and difference are not real, nor are they of the nature of qualities (*guṇa*) or activities (*karman*). Detailed explanation:
If one does not state the qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇadharma*), it contradicts the subject (*dharmin*), which constitutes a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*).
Regarding the statement "there is a dharma," you clearly do not admit it yourself.
Now, since the dharma is contradicted,
how can there be the fault of contradicting one's own words?
If even a concise statement were to constitute a fallacy,

then the syllogism cited by Īśvarasena in the *Hetuvidyā* (Nyāyamukha)— which possesses a reason contradictory to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the subject (*dharmin*)— should not be considered a valid refutation.
Furthermore, there is the fault of contradicting one's own words.
Since that [contradiction] does not apply here, how can this be a fault?
Nevertheless, he alters his position, saying: "The existence of identity and difference in you is not without reason."
If one were to cite the full text of the treatise as the *dharmin* (the subject of the proposition), one should follow the commentary (*ṭīkā*). Regarding the passage in the commentary stating,
"Now, as for the thesis (*pakṣa*), it should be distinguished separately":
If one were to proceed directly based on the treatise without making such distinctions,
there would be fallacies such as the property (dharma) becoming the locus of properties (dharmin),
because qualities (guṇa) and actions (karman) would both be included within the locus itself.
Furthermore, because it is used as a further analogy,
this fault arises.
[Commentary:]
Regarding the statement here that "the phrase 'ultimately real' constitutes the thesis," this refers to what is said in the treatise:
"Let it not be the case that these [substances] are also not real, nor qualities, nor activities.
This does not refer back to the three—real, quality, and activity—mentioned above.
That [objection] merely constitutes a general negation,
for it is a refutation based on non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).
As for the phrase "because they are distinct," this explains the meaning of the specific thesis (*pakṣa*) contained in the subsequent sentence.
The *yi* (intention) thus clarifies that within the treatises there is no principle of a "total measure" (*zongliang*).
The commentary states that the term "etc. includes qualities (*guṇa*), examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), and so forth.
There is an interpretation that [the term] "also" (api) serves as the example for the general thesis (*sāmānya-pakṣa*).
This is because the example of the general thesis is not a substance (*dravya*), a quality (*guṇa*), or an activity (*karman*).
It separately takes the category of inherence (*samavāya*) as the example. To explain in detail:
Since the treatise contains no refutation of the general thesis (*pakṣa*) and so forth,
nor any general example (*dṛṣṭānta*),
for what purpose is the example established?
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "should not be actual ground," the expression "not actual ground" encompasses two meanings.
First, it is not the ground of ultimate reality;
second, it is not the ground within the words of reality.
Commentary.
However, the text only provides examples where the nature (*svabhāva*) is identical to the substance (*dravya*).

To examine this in detail: according to the intent of the treatise, it is intended that substance, quality (*guṇa*), and activity (*karman*) share the same identity as the commonality (*sāmānya*) and particularity (*viśeṣa*), rather than establishing a separate nature for them.
This is because [the opponent] uses a real entity as the basis for the commonality of the example. Furthermore, the Commentary states:
"It is difficult to compel [them] to abandon the notion that there is no commonality or difference between the real entity and so forth.
Now, in our analysis of the treatise, we judge that the nature is identical to the real entity.
This must be a scribal error.
The *Śāstra* states:
"There is no other great [principle] that is not of the nature of reality."

The nine propositions together constitute a single nature, which is called "Great. Question: Why is this objection raised? Answer: That [opponent] establishes the nature of identity and difference based on similarity;
yet all nine [propositions] are unreal.
Because it is not truly similar,
it is difficult to establish that the Great [Vehicle] lacks true reality.
Commentary.
If it were not so, and one were to reach the point of committing an offense by assisting another in transgression, there are two interpretations.
One says: if one does not directly reprimand them in such a manner...
He [the opponent] grants that there is a non-reality upon each of the nine positions;

this is consistent [with our view]. Second, it is said: if one does not raise a general objection against the nine positions as a whole, but instead establishes a single great non-reality for them collectively.
This would then involve a contradiction,
because others maintain that all qualities (guṇas) are established as non-substantial; if,
in the case of the nine categories, the "Great" were non-substantial in nature.
Since he did not permit this, there is no correspondence [between the two].
The former interpretation is the primary one.
(Commentary)
Regarding the first five phrases, which concern that which is apprehended by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
there is one interpretation:

Commentary:
As for the statement that "feeling, pleasure, and so forth are also among the eight factors," there are dharmas that are designated as "dharmas."
Regarding the commentary’s statement, "There is the fault of partial conformity," some maintain that the term "condition" (*pratyaya*) is used to exclude the fault of total conformity.
This is unreasonable.
One should ask them:
"Is it excluded from among those things that possess dharmas, such as cognition and so forth?"
If it is by means of a restriction, why are they mutually consistent?
If it is not by means of a restriction,
then even if one were to establish a statement of conditions, how could it possibly preclude the restriction?
For this reason, one should immediately exclude [the category of] "concordant" (sādharmya).
Within the subject (dharmin), one first excludes cognition and so forth. To explain in detail:
the intent of this objection is as follows.
The treatise states that the term "condition" (*pratyaya*) occurs within the category of "factors" (*dharma*).
How, then, can one use a factor to exclude the fault of having a "possessor of factors" (*dharmī*)?
For this reason, it should be stated that within the category of "possessors of factors," [the term] excludes cognition and so forth.
Thus, there would be no correspondence.
Now, if we examine this through reasoning,
what loss is there in making such a distinction?
By drawing such analogies, one may attain awakening. For instance,
when the Buddha-dharma establishes the impermanence of sound against the proponents of phonetics (Śabdanaya),
the thesis (*pakṣa*) is that sound is impermanent.
One must thus distinguish the meaning of permanence as it pertains to sound.
If one does not so distinguish, then if another were to accept that sound is permanent, would this not be consistent?
Since there is no such consistency [in the absence of distinction], we know that [the qualification] is capable of making the distinction.
Now, within the "phenomenon" (dharma) that possesses attributes, both the subjective perceiver and the objective perceived are contained.
When the term "perceived" (ālambana) is used within the context of a phenomenon,
the intention is to exclude the subject— the perceiver— such as the Buddha and others.
What difference is there from the school that establishes sound as [inherently] existent?
Since it alone is not accepted,
the phrase "a single object-condition" (ekālambana) serves both to state the position and to exclude the "conformity" (anuvāda) [of the opponent].
I believe there is no error;
please examine this carefully.
[End of] Commentary.

Regarding the statement that "it reaches the point of explaining only the word," according to the intent of this passage, it appears to be restating an external objection. The meaning of the external objection is as follows:
since they already admit the existence of a mind that takes only the real (vastu) as its object.
In the treatise, the two characters "only-conditioning" (yùán) should be inserted.
By saying "only-conditioning," one excludes [factors such as] cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth;
thus, there is no fault of inconsistency.
The object-condition reveals the cognizing subject;
thus, there is no fault of contradicting our tenet.
(Commentary)
Regarding the statement "the universal cognition takes both as its object because it is attained through direct perception":
since it is already admitted that a single mind simultaneously takes two objects as its objects,
the two objects are mutually dependent.
This separation and non-separation are real entities perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Why is this so?
Because a single mind cannot be divided into two parts.
Therefore, these two objects mutually follow one another;
they are termed "separated" or "not separated" as obtained through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For this reason, the word "only" (*eva*) is used to exclude that which cannot be so obtained.
Commentary:
Regarding the phrase "because that which takes [them] collectively as its object is also excluded," this means that within the collective object,

It is also included among those things to be refuted.
Therefore, the word "conditioned" (*ālambana*) in the treatise eliminates all such faults. [End of] Treatise.

The Vedic masters say that from the navel of Nārāyaṇa a great lotus arose,
and from that lotus was born Brahmā, the progenitor.
That Brahmā creates all living beings and insentient things.
From the mouth of Brahmā, the brāhmaṇas are born;
from his two arms, the kṣatriyas are born.
From between the two thighs the Vaiśyas are born;
from the two feet the Śūdras are born.
The entire great earth is a sacrificial ground for the cultivation of merit and virtue.
He produced all manner of flowers and grasses as offerings.
He conjured up wild birds and beasts, as well as humans, pigs, sheep, and other such creatures from among men;
he then slaughtered them at the site of the precepts (śīma-kaṇḍa) to offer them to Brahmā.
To be born in that place is called nirvāṇa. Regarding the term "time," it refers to the proponents of the theory of time (Kālavādins),
who speak as follows.
When it is time for all things to ripen, they ripen;
when it is time for all things to scatter, they scatter.
Therefore, I say in my treatise:
Just as when one is struck by arrows or bows, death does not occur until the time has arrived;
yet when the time arrives, even the touch of a blade of grass causes death.
All things arise according to their time.
It ripens at its time;
it ceases at its time;
one cannot transcend its time.
Therefore, time constantly produces all things. As for the term "direction" (dis),
it refers to the proponents of the theory of direction (digvādins), who speak as follows.
In the beginning, the various directions arose;
from the various directions, the people of the world were born;
and from humans, heaven and earth came into being.
When heaven and earth perish and dissolve back into that place, it is called nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is eternally constant. As for the term "original limit" (pūrvakoṭi), it refers to the original birth.
The master Ānanda says:
Originally there were no sun, moon, stars, sky, or earth;
there was only fire and water.
At that time, Daṇḍa was born like a chicken egg,
golden in color all around;

One section is above, forming the heavens;
one section is below, forming the earth.
Between these two, the Brahmā Heaven arises.
He is named the grandfather of all sentient beings.
He creates all things, whether animate or inanimate.
When such things as these disperse and vanish into that state, it is called Nirvana. As for the term "spontaneous" (svayambhū):
That is to say, the proponents of the doctrine of no-cause (ahetu-vādin) speak thus:
"All things arise without cause and without condition."
There is no cause or condition for defilement or purity,
as stated in my treatise:

they exist spontaneously.
That which does not arise from causes is called nirvāṇa.
"Nature is permanent;

space is produced first."

from wind arises fire;
from fire arises smoke.
